da-2024-da-30.approach: One comparison with the middle element either finds the key or discards the middle and one half; in the worst case we recurse on the larger remaining half, of size at most $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$.

steps.title: One probe, then one half
steps.body: Compare the key with $A[m]$, $m = \lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor$ (0-based). If it is not equal, the search continues **only** in the left part ($\lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor$ elements) or the right part ($\lceil (n-1)/2 \rceil = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ elements).

steps.title: Worst case
steps.body:
The worst case takes the larger part, which has $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ elements, so
$$F(n) = 1 + F(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor), \qquad F(1) = 1.$$
Unrolling: $F(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$.

steps.title: Check with $n = 7$
steps.body: $F(7) = 1 + F(3) = 1 + 1 + F(1) = 3 = \lfloor \log_2 7 \rfloor + 1$. Searching $[1..7]$ for $7$: probes $4, 6, 7$ — exactly 3 comparisons. ✔

optionAnalysis.reason: One comparison plus a recursive search in at most half of the array.
That would search **both** halves (merge-sort–like recurrence, giving $\Theta(n)$); binary search discards one half.
Drops the comparison made at the current level, so it would give $F(n) = F(1)$ for all $n$.
That is linear search: each comparison removes only one element, giving $F(n) = n$.

pitfalls: Confusing the binary-search recurrence with the divide-and-conquer recurrence of merge sort (option B).
da-2024-da-30.verification: Unrolled the recurrence to $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor + 1$, the known worst case, and checked $n = 7$ by hand.

da-2024-da-31.approach: Read the recursion as a two-pointer loop: swap the ends, move both pointers inward, stop when they meet or cross. That is the classic in-place reversal.

steps.title: What one call does
steps.body: If $s_1 < s_2$: swap $D[s_1]$ and $D[s_2]$, then recurse on $(s_1+1,\ s_2-1)$. Otherwise do nothing.

steps.title: Unroll the calls
steps.body: The swapped pairs are $(s_1, s_2), (s_1+1, s_2-1), (s_1+2, s_2-2), \dots$ until the indices meet (odd length: middle element untouched) or cross (even length). Every element at offset $k$ from $s_1$ is exchanged with the element at offset $k$ from $s_2$.

optionAnalysis.reason: No comparisons are made and nothing is returned; it only swaps.
No comparisons, so it cannot sort; e.g. a sorted segment becomes descending.
Swapping symmetric pairs from the outside in reverses the segment.
The recursive call keeps swapping the inner pairs too, so the other elements do change (unless the segment has length ≤ 3).

pitfalls: Reading only the first swap and missing the recursive call (option D).

da-2024-da-34.approach: Simulate both searches on the actual state numbers. Because ties are broken by the smallest number and every child is larger than its parent, both strategies pick the same state each time.

steps.title: BFS
steps.body:
Queue (FIFO), smallest number first:
- expand 1 → add 2, 3
- expand 2 → add 4 (3 already queued)
- expand 3 → add 5
- expand 4 → add 6
- expand 5 → add 7
- next is 6 = goal.

Expanded: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ → **5 states**.

steps.title: DFS
steps.body:
Stack (LIFO), children of the newest state taken smallest first:
- expand 1 → 2, 3; take 2
- expand 2 → 3, 4; take 3
- expand 3 → 4, 5; take 4
- expand 4 → 5, 6; take 5
- expand 5 → 6, 7; take 6 = goal.

Expanded: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ → **5 states**.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: Both expand the same sequence $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ before reaching 6. (If the goal test is done at generation instead, both stop after expanding $1,2,3,4$ — still equal.)

answer.value: Both expand the **same** number of states (5) — option (C)

DFS also expands exactly 5 states.

steps.title: Selection sort

Pass 2: minimum of $[3,2,4,5]$ is 2 → swap with index 1: $[1,2,3,4,5]$ — **sorted**.

da-2024-da-36.approach: An FD $\alpha \to \beta$ is derivable iff $\beta \subseteq \alpha^+$. Only two left-hand sides occur in the options, $VW$ and $WX$, so compute those two closures.

steps.title: Closure of $VW$
steps.body:
Start $\{V, W\}$.
- $V \to X$ adds $X$: $\{V, W, X\}$
- $WX \to Y$, $WX \to Z$ add $Y, Z$: $\{V, W, X, Y, Z\}$
- $U$ is on the right of no FD, so it never enters.

$(VW)^+ = \{V, W, X, Y, Z\}$.

steps.title: Closure of $WX$
steps.body: Start $\{W, X\}$; $WX \to Y, Z$ gives $(WX)^+ = \{W, X, Y, Z\}$.

steps.title: Check the options
steps.body:
| FD | Test | Derivable? |
|---|---|---|
| $VW \to YZ$ | $YZ \subseteq (VW)^+$ | yes |
| $WX \to YZ$ | $YZ \subseteq (WX)^+$ | yes (union rule) |
| $VW \to U$ | $U \notin (VW)^+$ | no |
| $VW \to Y$ | $Y \in (VW)^+$ | yes |

optionAnalysis.reason: $(VW)^+ = \{V,W,X,Y,Z\} \supseteq \{Y,Z\}$.
Union of the given $WX \to Y$ and $WX \to Z$.
No FD has $U$ on its right side, so only $U$ itself can determine $U$.
$Y \in (VW)^+$ (via $V \to X$, then $WX \to Y$).

pitfalls: Reversing $U \to V, U \to W$ to conclude $VW \to U$ — FDs are not symmetric.
da-2024-da-36.verification: $U$ never appears on a right-hand side, so $U$ is in every key and no FD without $U$ on the left can derive it; the others follow by pseudo-transitivity ($V \to X$ with $WX \to YZ$ gives $VW \to YZ$).

da-2024-da-37.approach: A subset is a subspace iff it contains $\mathbf{0}$ and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Spans and solution sets of homogeneous systems always are; sets with squared coefficients or a nonzero constant term fail.

steps.title: (A) a span
steps.body: It is $\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,0)^T, (1,0,0)^T\}$ with arbitrary real $\alpha, \beta$ — every span is a subspace (here the plane $x_3 = 0$). ✔

steps.title: (B) squared coefficients
steps.body: $\alpha^2, \beta^2 \ge 0$, so the set is the cone $\{a(1,2,0)^T + b(1,0,1)^T : a, b \ge 0\}$. It contains $(1,2,0)^T$ but not $-(1,2,0)^T$ (that would need $a = -1 < 0$, since the two vectors are independent). Not closed under scalar multiplication. ✘

steps.title: (C) homogeneous system
steps.body: It is the null space of $\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$; null spaces are subspaces (a line through the origin here). ✔

steps.title: (D) non-homogeneous
steps.body: $\mathbf{0}$ gives $5\cdot0 + 2\cdot0 + 4 = 4 \ne 0$, so $\mathbf{0}$ is not in the set. ✘

optionAnalysis.reason: Span of two vectors with unrestricted coefficients.
Coefficients $\alpha^2, \beta^2$ are non-negative, so negatives of members are missing.
Solution set of a homogeneous linear system (null space).
Affine plane not through the origin ($+4$ constant).

pitfalls: Treating (B) as a span because $\alpha, \beta$ range over $\mathbb{R}$ — the squares do not.
da-2024-da-37.verification: Zero-vector test: A ($\alpha=\beta=0$), B ($\alpha=\beta=0$), C pass, D fails; B then fails closure under multiplication by $-1$.

da-2024-da-38.approach: For a fixed $M$, every consistent system $M\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has the same number of solutions: unique iff $\operatorname{null}(M) = \{\mathbf 0\}$ (rank = number of columns), infinite otherwise. Whether it is consistent depends on $\mathbf b$ lying in the column space.

steps.title: Key fact
steps.body: If $M\mathbf{x}_0 = \mathbf{b}$, all solutions are $\mathbf{x}_0 + \operatorname{null}(M)$. So "unique" and "infinite" can never occur together for the same $M$; "no solution" vs "some solution" depends only on whether $\mathbf{b} \in \operatorname{col}(M)$.

steps.title: (A) and (C) are impossible
steps.body:
(A) needs $\operatorname{null}(M) = \{\mathbf 0\}$ for $\mathbf p$ and $\ne \{\mathbf 0\}$ for $\mathbf q$ — contradiction.
(C) $M$ is $2\times3$: $\operatorname{rank} \le 2 < 3$, so $\dim \operatorname{null}(M) \ge 1$ and a unique solution is impossible.

steps.title: (B) example
steps.body: $M = \begin{bmatrix} 1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&0 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf p = (0,0,1)^T$ (third equation $0 = 1$: no solution), $\mathbf q = (0,0,0)^T$ (solutions $(0,0,t)^T$: infinitely many). ✔

steps.title: (D) example
steps.body: $M = \begin{bmatrix} 1&0\\0&1\\0&0 \end{bmatrix}$ (rank 2 = columns, null space $\{\mathbf 0\}$), $\mathbf p = (1,2,0)^T$ gives the unique $\mathbf x = (1,2)^T$; $\mathbf q = (0,0,1)^T \notin \operatorname{col}(M)$ gives no solution. ✔

optionAnalysis.reason: A unique solution forces $\operatorname{null}(M) = \{\mathbf 0\}$, so no right-hand side can give infinitely many.
Singular $M$: $\mathbf p$ outside the column space, $\mathbf q$ inside.
A wide $2 \times 3$ matrix always has a non-trivial null space.

da-2024-da-39.approach: A projection onto $U$ fixes every vector of $U$ and is idempotent; its range is $U$, so rank–nullity gives the null-space dimension $3 - \dim U$.

steps.title: Idempotence
steps.body: $M\mathbf v \in U$ and $M$ fixes vectors of $U$, so $M(M\mathbf v) = M\mathbf v$ for all $\mathbf v$: $M^2 = M$. Then $M^3 = M^2 \cdot M = M \cdot M = M^2 = M$. So (C) and (D) hold.

steps.title: Null space dimension
steps.body:
$\operatorname{range}(M) = U$, so $\operatorname{rank}(M) = \dim U$ and
$$\dim \operatorname{null}(M) = 3 - \dim U.$$
- $\dim U = 1$: nullity $= 3 - 1 = 2$ → (A) false.
- $\dim U = 2$: nullity $= 3 - 2 = 1$ → (B) true.

steps.title: Example
steps.body: Projection onto the $x_1x_2$-plane: $M = \operatorname{diag}(1,1,0)$; null space is the $x_3$-axis (1-D), $M^2 = M^3 = M$. Onto the $x_1$-axis: $M = \operatorname{diag}(1,0,0)$, null space is the $x_2x_3$-plane (2-D).

optionAnalysis.reason: Nullity $= 3 - 1 = 2$, not 1.
Nullity $= 3 - 2 = 1$.
Projecting twice is the same as projecting once.
$M^3 = M \cdot M^2 = M \cdot M = M$.

pitfalls: Equating the null-space dimension with $\dim U$ instead of $3 - \dim U$.

da-2024-da-42.approach: Use the two extreme binary trees of height $H$ (height = edges on the longest root-to-leaf path): the path (chain) and the perfect tree. They give the tight bounds; a counter-example from the chain kills (D).

steps.title: (A) $L \le I + 1$
steps.body: Let $n_0, n_1, n_2$ count nodes with 0, 1, 2 children. Edges: $N - 1 = n_1 + 2n_2$ and $N = n_0 + n_1 + n_2$ give $n_0 = n_2 + 1$. So $L = n_2 + 1 \le (n_1 + n_2) + 1 = I + 1$. ✔ (Single node: $L = 1, I = 0$.)

steps.title: (B) bounds on $N$
steps.body: A height-$H$ tree has a root-to-leaf path with $H + 1$ nodes, so $N \ge H + 1$. Level $k$ has at most $2^k$ nodes: $N \le \sum_{k=0}^{H} 2^k = 2^{H+1} - 1$. ✔

steps.title: (C) bounds on $I$
steps.body: The $H$ non-leaf nodes on the longest path are internal, so $I \ge H$. Internal nodes lie on levels $0..H-1$: $I \le \sum_{k=0}^{H-1} 2^k = 2^H - 1$. ✔

steps.title: (D) fails
steps.body: Leaves lie on levels $\le H$, so the right bound would be $L \le 2^H$, not $2^{H-1}$; and the lower bound fails too: a chain of height $H = 3$ has $L = 1 < 3$. Also a perfect tree with $H = 1$ has $L = 2 > 2^{0} = 1$. ✘

optionAnalysis.reason: Chain gives the lower bound, perfect tree the upper bound.
Chain has exactly $H$ internal nodes; perfect tree has $2^H - 1$.
A chain has one leaf, so $H \le L$ fails for $H \ge 2$; the upper bound should be $2^H$.

pitfalls: Mixing up height measured in edges with height measured in levels (nodes).
da-2024-da-42.verification: Checked all four statements on the chain of height 3 ($N=4, I=3, L=1$) and the perfect tree of height 2 ($N=7, I=3, L=4$): A, B, C hold in both; D fails on the chain and on the perfect tree of height 1.
